frozen_original.title: AG Pam Bondi Files Misconduct Complaint Against Judge Boasberg; Admin Uses Shadow Docket 34 Times
frozen_original.synopsis: Attorney General Pam Bondi filed a formal judicial misconduct complaint against Chief Judge James Boasberg after he held the administration in contempt for defying its order halting deportations under the Alien Enemies Act. A Brennan Center analysis found that as of March 2026 the Trump administration had invoked the Supreme Court's emergency shadow docket 34 times in 14 months — more than the Biden, Obama, and George W. Bush administrations combined — winning 80% of those emergency requests.

children.title: DOJ Files Judicial-Misconduct Complaint Against Judge James Boasberg
children.description_short: The Justice Department filed a misconduct complaint against Judge Boasberg on July 29, 2025; the Sixth Circuit dismissed it in December.
children.description_medium: On July 29, 2025, the Justice Department filed a judicial-misconduct complaint against Chief Judge James Boasberg with the D.C. Circuit’s Judicial Council. The complaint alleged misconduct based on remarks at a March Judicial Conference and Boasberg’s handling of litigation over removals under the Alien Enemies Act. A Sixth Circuit order later dismissed it, citing insufficient evidence and other Rule 11 grounds; the allegations were not findings against Boasberg.
children.description_long: On July 29, 2025, the Justice Department filed a judicial-misconduct complaint against Chief Judge James Boasberg with the D.C. Circuit’s Judicial Council. The complaint alleged that comments Boasberg reportedly made during a March Judicial Conference and his rulings in litigation over removals under the Alien Enemies Act violated judicial ethics canons. Those statements were allegations in the complaint, not findings. After the proceeding was transferred to the Sixth Circuit, Chief Judge Jeffrey Sutton dismissed it on December 19, 2025. The order said the complaint lacked sufficient evidence and was related in part to the merits of rulings; it also noted that DOJ had not supplied an attachment it cited as evidence. The order resolved the misconduct complaint, not the separate underlying deportation litigation. Reuters reported the filing on July 28, while the Sixth Circuit order gives July 29 as the filing date; this card uses the court’s date. The complaint’s dismissal is stated without implying that Boasberg committed misconduct or that the underlying litigation ended on that date.

children.title: Trump Administration Makes 34 Emergency Requests to the Supreme Court by March 2026
children.description_short: A Brennan Center tally says the administration sought emergency Supreme Court intervention 34 times by March 2026; 25 requests had decisions, with an 80% win rate.
children.description_medium: A Brennan Center tally published April 28, 2026, reported that by March the second Trump administration had asked the Supreme Court to intervene 34 times when lower courts blocked parts of its agenda. The Court had issued 25 shadow-docket decisions on those requests and ruled for the administration in 80 percent of them. These are the Center’s counts; they do not establish that each request produced a final merits judgment or a lasting policy change.
children.description_long: By March 2026, the second Trump administration had asked the Supreme Court to intervene 34 times after lower courts blocked parts of its agenda, according to a Brennan Center for Justice tally published April 28, 2026. The Center reported that the Court issued 25 shadow-docket decisions on those requests and ruled for the administration in 80 percent of them. This is a count of emergency requests and resulting decisions, not a count of final merits judgments or proof that every requested policy became permanent. The reported win rate has 25 decisions as its denominator; the source does not claim that all 34 requests received decisions by that date. Because this record combines separate matters from the Boasberg complaint, it treats the tally as a distinct administration-wide pattern over time. The applications’ use of an established emergency process does not alone show misconduct, and the count does not supply individual case outcomes or quantified harms. It is attributed to the Brennan Center, whose policy article advances reforms to Supreme Court practice. The card therefore records its measure and scope without presenting the Center’s characterization of the docket as a court finding.

frozen_original.synopsis: Through a combination of Schedule F reinstatement and supplementary executive orders, the Trump administration removed civil service protections from an estimated 50,000 or more federal employees across agencies by January 20, 2025. The affected employees spanned national security agencies, regulatory bodies, law enforcement, and scientific agencies. The action was the largest single rollback of the merit-based civil service system in the history of the United States federal government.

primary.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14171, “Restoring Accountability to Policy-Influencing Positions Within the Federal Workforce.” The order revived and amended the earlier Schedule F framework, renaming the category Schedule Policy/Career. The official rule description says it applies to a limited set of policy-influencing positions that are confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating. OPM later implemented the category through rulemaking; its description says covered roles remain career positions but are no longer subject to the same removal procedures. The order’s signature was a completed presidential action, but it does not establish that 50,000 employees had already been reclassified or lost protections on that date. The original entry’s estimate of 50,000-plus employees, claim of immediate removals across agencies, and “largest single rollback” characterization are therefore excluded. This record focuses on the order and the limited category it created, with later implementation treated as subsequent context. The number of positions ultimately designated and the number of employees actually affected are not established by the sources reviewed.
